clue.text: Old Greek has one in stock? Not quite

indicators.note: the word in tells us the numeral goes inside the shortened word
not quite the whole word, so the final letter of stock is dropped

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A question about whether an ancient Greek keeps a single item in his store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' trims STOCK to STOC; 'in' then puts I (one) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Zeno's philosophy of the Porch was an ancient Greek thinker.

clue.text: Swimmer foiling efforts to catch him?

definitions.text: Swimmer foiling efforts to catch him?

parts.words: Swimmer foiling efforts to catch him?
parts.note: a sea creature that might parry an angler like a fencer with a foil, since its snout is a blade

explanation.surface: A fish that thwarts anglers trying to land it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foiling' reads as thwarting, but a foil is a fencing blade, and this swimmer carries a long blade on its nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A large ocean game fish with a long flat bill like a blade.

clue.text: Fox turning head frequently

indicators.note: the head, the first two letters, is turned round

parts.note: fox written as F, O and then X, the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: A fox that keeps looking round.
explanation.walkthrough: Read FOX as FO plus X, and X as the Roman numeral TEN; 'turning head' swaps FO to OF, giving OF + TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Many times, again and again, means frequently.

clue.text: Talking bird

parts.note: a bird that chats away; the name is also given to birds such as the waxwing

explanation.surface: A parrot or mynah that can speak.
explanation.definitionFit: One who talks incessantly, a name also applied to certain noisy birds.

clue.text: Builder's plot to wall in a William Bowman, revolutionary

indicators.note: to wall in means to enclose, so the plot surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: a builder's plot is a building site
William Tell, the legendary Swiss archer who shot an apple from his son's head

explanation.surface: A builder means to enclose a plot around an archer, who turns out to be a revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as a rebel (Tell was one), but here it is a noun for something that revolves, an orbiting body.
explanation.definitionFit: A moon or spacecraft revolves around a planet, so it is literally a thing that revolves.

clue.text: What one very quietly did in a snow vehicle

definitions.text: What one very quietly did in a snow vehicle

indicators.note: in means the musical marking goes inside the vehicle

parts.note: a sled runs on snow
one is the Roman numeral I
pp (pianissimo) is the musical marking for very quietly

explanation.surface: Someone sneaking off very quietly on a sledge.
explanation.walkthrough: I (one) and PP go inside SLED; and to steal off very quietly is what the whole clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving away unnoticed or sliding on snow are both senses of going quietly or smoothly.

clue.text: In which we see Miranda, or Marie

definitions.meaning: Miranda is Prospero's daughter in Shakespeare's last solo play
Dame Marie, a celebrated English stage actress of the early twentieth century

explanation.surface: Naming the play in which either of two women might appear.
explanation.walkthrough: Miranda is the heroine of Shakespeare's The Tempest; Dame Marie Tempest was a famous actress, so 'or Marie' is a second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's storm play features Miranda, and Dame Marie was an Edwardian stage star of that surname.

clue.text: Serve soup for old Harry's supper companion?

definitions.meaning: to dish soup out with a big spoon
Old Harry is the devil, and he who sups with the devil needs a long spoon

explanation.surface: Dishing out soup for an elderly man's supper guest.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Harry is a nickname for the devil; the proverb says whoever sups with the devil should have a long spoon.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-handled spoon serves soup, and the proverb's long spoon is what you need at the devil's table.

clue.text: Put in What could make one priest …

indicators.note: the clue asks what the letters could be made into, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: An interjection breaking off with the question of how a man becomes a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of ONE PRIEST rearrange to give the answer; the ellipsis carries the priest on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To insert something between, or interject a remark, is to put it in.

clue.text: … wear this (note physical education set-up)

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means read from bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: doh is a note of the tonic sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: priests dress in this, with a bracketed aside about gym.
explanation.walkthrough: Following on from 7, 'wear this' means what a priest wears: the linen vestment of Jewish priests in the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: The sleeveless vestment worn by priests of ancient Israel, described in Exodus.

clue.text: Exile for East German ethnic prejudice

parts.note: Ost is the German word for east
prejudice against people of another race

explanation.surface: Banishment as the punishment for an East German guilty of bigotry.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Athens citizens were banished by vote, and the word now means being shut out by society.

clue.text: Dear old Mrs Chevalier!

parts.note: the music-hall singer Albert Chevalier's song 'My Old ...' calls his wife by a cockney term of endearment

explanation.surface: An affectionate tribute to the wife of a Frenchman called Chevalier.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert Chevalier was a Victorian cockney music-hall star; his famous song is 'My Old Dutch', where 'Dutch' (from 'duchess') is rhyming-slang-style cockney for one's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney slang for a wife, from duchess, made famous by Chevalier's song about his own spouse.

clue.text: The fellow at the film studio

definitions.text: The fellow at the film studio

parts.note: a don is a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.surface: Someone asking which man works at the film studio.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Donat was a British film star of the 1930s and 40s (The 39 Steps, Goodbye, Mr Chips).
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Donat was a leading actor of British cinema, a man found working at the studios.

clue.text: Promoted Whistler — was wrong, soft in the head

indicators.note: in the head means placed at the front, before the other pieces

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
a referee blows a whistle, so a whistler is a ref
erred means was wrong

explanation.surface: A referee who got the job despite his mistakes and his feeble wits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistler' suggests the painter, but it is the referee; 'soft in the head' looks like an insult but places P at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone advanced to higher rank was, in older usage, raised in office.

clue.text: Pent (pace Lovelace)

parts.note: shut up behind walls, despite Lovelace's line that stone walls do not a prison make

explanation.surface: A note that someone is confined, with apologies to a Cavalier poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Pace means 'with respect to (a person who disagrees)'. Richard Lovelace wrote 'Stone walls do not a prison make'; the answer means walled up, which he would deny is imprisonment.
explanation.definitionFit: Being walled in, from Latin murus a wall, is to be shut up and confined.

clue.text: Second house he missed of great consequence

parts.note: a second is a moment

indicators.note: missed means the letters are left out of the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A moment when a man missed his house, which turned out to matter a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly significant, of great importance.

clue.text: Pony hot and bothered, blowing furiously

indicators.note: hot and bothered means flustered, so the letters are flustered into a new order

explanation.surface: A pony that is overheated and agitated, panting hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot and bothered' looks like a single phrase about the pony, but 'hot' is fodder and 'and bothered' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical cyclone of the western Pacific is a storm of violent winds.

clue.text: Peter includes Eugene in the Maths line

indicators.note: includes means the name holds the other name inside it

parts.note: taken as written
Eugene Aram, the 18th-century schoolmaster and murderer of Bulwer-Lytton's novel

explanation.surface: A teacher named Peter brings his colleague Eugene into the mathematics department.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Aram was a famous schoolmaster murderer (Hood's poem, Bulwer-Lytton's novel), so 'Eugene' gives ARAM, cut into PETER after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A constant or variable in an equation is a term found in mathematics.

clue.text: Intelligence about terrible riot — O infamous!

indicators.note: about means the word for intelligence goes round the other letters

parts.note: nous is common sense or intelligence

indicators.note: terrible means the letters are in a terrible mess, so rearranged

parts.note: the word riot followed by the exclamation O (printed as a dash and O), five letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: News of an appalling uprising, with a cry at its shameful nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' shuffles RIOT and O into TORIO, which 'about' puts inside NOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Well known for something bad is the meaning of infamous.

clue.text: Coming straight from the shoulder it sounds funny

indicators.note: it sounds tells us the word for funny is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: humorous means funny

explanation.surface: A remark delivered bluntly that nonetheless sounds amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight from the shoulder' is an idiom for frank speech, but here it is anatomical: the bone that runs from shoulder to elbow, also known as the funny bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper-arm bone runs straight down from the shoulder joint to the elbow.

clue.text: Barber's speciality — make-believe teddy-bear cut

parts.note: sham means pretend or make-believe

indicators.note: cut means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is A. A. Milne's teddy bear

explanation.surface: A barber offering a pretend haircut to a child's teddy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' suggests the haircut, but it docks the last letter of POOH.
explanation.definitionFit: A hair wash is a service a barber offers.

clue.text: Sign of a number entering harbour

indicators.note: entering means the number goes inside the word for harbour

parts.note: a port is a harbour
ten is a number

explanation.surface: A signal from a ship as it comes into harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign of something to come.

clue.text: What should offenders do if caught by coppers?

indicators.note: caught by means the word is held inside the coins

parts.note: coppers are pennies, pence
an is an archaic word for if

explanation.surface: Asking what criminals should do once the police have arrested them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police, but means copper coins; AN is an old form of 'if', as in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinners are expected to do an act of atonement for wrongdoing.

clue.text: New order for cartons in force

indicators.note: a new order for the letters means they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Boxes being reordered in quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: To compel or oblige someone is to force them.

clue.text: Oil mixed in small volume for the gripes.

indicators.note: in means the mixed letters go inside the unit of volume

parts.note: cc, a cubic centimetre, is a small volume

indicators.note: mixed means the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A dose of oil mixed into a small measure as a remedy for stomach pains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' turns OIL into OLI, which goes 'in' CC.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe abdominal pain, colloquially the gripes.

clue.text: Sample Simple Simon sought

definitions.meaning: to try a little of something
in the nursery rhyme Simple Simon says to the pieman 'Let me ... your ware'

explanation.surface: A reference to what the nursery-rhyme simpleton wanted from the pieman.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme, Simple Simon met a pieman and asked to try his wares, without a penny to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: To try a small portion is to sample it, which Simple Simon wanted from the pieman's pies.

clue.text: Wealthiest among Hugo's wretches?

parts.note: Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables, the wretched; a hoarder of money is a wretch who is rich

explanation.surface: Asking which of the characters in Victor Hugo's novel had the most money.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a hoarding skinflint is the start of misérables, and literally once meant a wretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder of wealth is a wretched, stingy person, from Latin for wretched.

clue.text: Boy raised in Sarum

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so backwards
in means only a piece found within the town's name is used

parts.note: Sarum is the old name for Salisbury

explanation.surface: A lad brought up in the old cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: SALIS sits in SALISBURY (Sarum); 'raised' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy's name, as in George Eliot's Silas Marner.

clue.text: French home town of a King of Arms

definitions.meaning: the city on the Rhône, in its traditional English spelling
Lyon King of Arms is Scotland's chief heraldic officer

explanation.surface: Asking which French town a heraldic official comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: France's second city, and the possessive of Scotland's Lord Lyon, the senior herald.

clue.text: Lit up in company? Violation of etiquette

indicators.note: a violation breaks something, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Is getting drunk in company a breach of good manners?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lit up' means drunk in the surface; the whole surface asks about a breach of manners, but the anagram gives a nice point of correct behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine point of etiquette or correct conduct, from Italian puntiglio, small point.

clue.text: Cases broken, and part of a cooking dish

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the word are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: Crates are smashed and a piece of crockery goes with them.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthenware pot for slow-cooking stews in the oven.

clue.text: Used to water them

parts.note: the perforated nozzle of a watering can shares its name with the garden flowers it sprinkles

explanation.surface: A gardener's remark about the can used on the flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The sprinkler head on a watering can is called a rose, so the flowers are watered with their namesakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden flowers are watered with the sprinkler head of a can, which bears the same name.
